pharm: Cyclic polypeptide calcineurin inhibitor; binds cyclophilin to inhibit calcineurin and reversibly suppress T-lymphocyte activation
tags: Boxed warning: malignancy, serious infection, nephrotoxicity
Modified and non-modified forms NOT bioequivalent
quick: Transplant ~6-9 mg/kg/day divided q12h titrated to trough; RA & psoriasis start 2.5 mg/kg/day BID (max 4 mg/kg/day)
Take on a consistent schedule re meals; avoid grapefruit/juice
Use only if needed; higher hypertension, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and low birth weight (often confounded by underlying disease)
Present in human milk; account for ethanol excipient and avoid extra alcohol; weigh benefit vs risk
Nephrotoxic; monitor creatinine and reduce dose. RA/psoriasis: contraindicated if renal function abnormal
Severe impairment lowers clearance; reduce dose to keep target trough
Avoid grapefruit; limit alcohol (capsules contain ethanol)
Whole-blood trough (TDM), creatinine/BP, K+, Mg, lipids, LFTs
summary: Ciclosporin (INN; US generic cyclosporine) is a calcineurin-inhibitor immunosuppressant indicated for prophylaxis of organ rejection in kidney, liver, and heart transplantation and for severe rheumatoid arthritis and severe recalcitrant plaque psoriasis. It carries a boxed warning: only physicians experienced in systemic immunosuppressive therapy (and in transplant management at transplant doses) should prescribe it, patients must be managed in adequately equipped facilities, and the drug increases susceptibility to serious/fatal infection and to malignancy (especially lymphoma and skin cancer) and causes dose-related structural nephrotoxicity with significant rises in serum creatinine. It has a narrow therapeutic index requiring whole-blood trough therapeutic drug monitoring. Critically, the modified (microemulsion) and non-modified (Sandimmune) formulations are NOT bioequivalent and cannot be interchanged without physician supervision. Common toxicities include nephrotoxicity, hypertension, tremor, hirsutism, gingival hyperplasia, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hyperlipidemia.
indications: Prophylaxis of organ rejection in kidney, liver, and heart allogeneic transplantation (with corticosteroids +/- azathioprine)
Severe active rheumatoid arthritis not adequately responsive to methotrexate (alone or combined with methotrexate)
Severe (extensive/disabling), recalcitrant plaque psoriasis in adult non-immunocompromised patients who have failed or cannot tolerate at least one systemic therapy

dosage.t: Initial oral dose may be given 4-12 h before or after transplant; titrate to target trough
dosage.n: Same initial dose as Sandimmune; modified gives greater exposure at same trough - monitor and adjust; reduce to maintenance

dosage.t: Titrate to predefined blood concentration; lower maintenance doses usually suffice
Titrate to target trough; clearance slightly slower in cardiac patients
dosage.n: Dose to clinical assessment of rejection and tolerability

dosage.d: Start 2.5 mg/kg/day, divided twice daily; may increase by 0.5-0.75 mg/kg/day after 8 and 12 weeks to a maximum of 4 mg/kg/day
dosage.t: Onset of action usually 4-8 weeks; discontinue if no benefit by 16 weeks
dosage.n: Decrease dose 25-50% to control hypertension or creatinine rise >=30% above baseline; NSAIDs/steroids may continue

dosage.d: Start 2.5 mg/kg/day (1.25 mg/kg twice daily); after 4 weeks may increase by ~0.5 mg/kg/day at 2-week intervals to a maximum of 4.0 mg/kg/day
dosage.t: Hold at starting dose >=4 weeks before titrating
dosage.n: Decrease dose 25-50% for hypertension or creatinine rise >=25% above pretreatment; no concomitant PUVA/UVB, methotrexate, other immunosuppressants, coal tar, or radiation

dosage.d: 1:1 mg-for-mg conversion by total daily dose when switching non-modified (Sandimmune) to modified
dosage.t: Follow trough more frequently after any switch
dosage.n: Modified and non-modified are NOT bioequivalent; modified yields higher exposure - never interchange without physician supervision

admin: Prescribe only under supervision of a physician experienced in systemic immunosuppressive therapy; at transplant doses only physicians experienced in transplant management, with adequate laboratory/supportive resources
Give the total daily dose as two divided doses (BID) on a consistent schedule with regard to time of day and relation to meals
Do not eat grapefruit or drink grapefruit juice while taking ciclosporin
Confirm the formulation at each refill - modified (microemulsion) and non-modified (Sandimmune) are not interchangeable without physician oversight

Oral solution: mix in a glass (not plastic) container with orange/apple juice (modified) at room temperature, stir well, drink at once, then rinse the container with more diluent and drink to ensure full dose; dry the syringe, do not rinse with water
Capsules contain ethanol as an excipient - account for this in pregnancy, lactation, and patients avoiding alcohol
Establish baseline blood pressure and twice-yearly (or more) renal function before and during therapy in RA/psoriasis patients
moa: Ciclosporin is a cyclic 11-amino-acid polypeptide that binds the cytosolic immunophilin cyclophilin; the ciclosporin-cyclophilin complex inhibits calcineurin, the calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase that activates nuclear factor of activated T-cells (NF-AT). This blocks transcription of interleukin-2 and other cytokines, producing specific, reversible inhibition of T-lymphocytes (preferentially T-helper cells) in the G0 and G1 phases of the cell cycle and suppressing cell-mediated immune responses such as allograft rejection and delayed hypersensitivity, with lesser effects on humoral immunity.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to ciclosporin or any formulation ingredient (including polyoxyl/Cremophor in IV form)
RA or psoriasis patients with abnormal renal function, uncontrolled hypertension, or malignancy
Psoriasis: concomitant PUVA or UVB phototherapy, methotrexate or other immunosuppressants, coal tar, or radiation therapy
relative: Active or prior malignancy, especially lymphoma or skin cancer
Concomitant potassium-sparing diuretics or high potassium intake (hyperkalemia)
monitor: Serum creatinine / renal function and blood pressure (baseline and serially)
Signs of infection and of malignancy (skin examination, lymphadenopathy)

preg: Published data over decades, including the Transplant Pregnancy Registry International, have not identified a drug-associated risk of major birth defects or miscarriage. However, hypertension, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, and low birth weight are increased in pregnancies exposed to ciclosporin, although the underlying maternal disease and concomitant medications confound interpretation. Animal embryo-fetal studies showed toxicity at doses below the maximum recommended human dose. The ethanol content of capsules/solution should be considered. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed and counsel on monitored risks; encourage Transplant Pregnancy Registry International enrollment.
lact: Ciclosporin and its metabolites are present in human milk after oral and intravenous administration. Adverse effects on the breastfed infant have not been reported and there are no data on milk production. The alcohol (ethanol) content of the capsule/solution formulation should be taken into account, and lactating women are encouraged to avoid additional alcohol intake during treatment. Weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's clinical need and potential infant risk.
renal: Ciclosporin undergoes minimal renal elimination (about 6% of dose in urine) and its pharmacokinetics are not significantly altered in end-stage renal disease on routine hemodialysis (<1% recovered in dialysate). However, it is intrinsically nephrotoxic and causes dose-related structural kidney damage; monitor renal function carefully and reduce the dose for rising creatinine. In rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis, patients with impaired/abnormal renal function should NOT receive ciclosporin. In transplantation, reduce dose for nephrotoxicity and distinguish drug toxicity from rejection.
hepatic: Ciclosporin is extensively metabolized by the liver (CYP3A). Clearance may be significantly reduced in severe liver disease, increasing exposure; the dose may need to be reduced in severe hepatic impairment to keep blood concentrations within the recommended target range. Monitor liver function tests and ciclosporin troughs closely.

major: CYP3A inhibitors that RAISE ciclosporin levels (nephrotoxicity/toxicity risk) - diltiazem, nicardipine, verapamil; azole antifungals fluconazole, itraconazole, ketoconazole, voriconazole; macrolides azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin; quinupristin/dalfopristin; danazol; nefazodone; metoclopramide; oral contraceptives; allopurinol, amiodarone, bromocriptine, colchicine, imatinib; HIV protease inhibitors (indinavir, nelfinavir, ritonavir, saquinavir)

CYP3A inducers that LOWER ciclosporin levels (rejection risk) - rifampin, nafcillin; carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin; bosentan, octreotide, orlistat, sulfinpyrazone, terbinafine, ticlopidine; St. John's Wort

Nephrotoxic drugs (additive/synergistic renal impairment) - aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin), vancomycin, amphotericin B, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, NSAIDs (diclofenac, naproxen, sulindac), fibrates, tacrolimus, colchicine, ranitidine
Potassium-sparing diuretics and high potassium (hyperkalemia) - do not use potassium-sparing diuretics
moderate: Ciclosporin raises levels/toxicity of other drugs - diclofenac, methotrexate, digoxin, colchicine, prednisolone, statins (rhabdomyolysis/myopathy risk), repaglinide, bosentan, dabigatran, sirolimus, aliskiren, NSAIDs
Statins - reduce statin dose; monitor for myopathy/rhabdomyolysis
HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors and fibrates together with ciclosporin increase myotoxicity risk
minor: Calcium channel blockers used for ciclosporin-associated hypertension may themselves alter ciclosporin metabolism
No clinically significant PK interaction with aspirin, ketoprofen, piroxicam, or indomethacin
interactions.food: Take on a consistent schedule with regard to meals. Grapefruit and grapefruit juice inhibit CYP3A and raise ciclosporin blood concentrations - avoid them. High potassium foods/salt substitutes can worsen hyperkalemia.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid grapefruit/grapefruit juice. Capsules and oral solution contain ethanol; lactating women and patients avoiding alcohol should account for this and avoid additional alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: May increase serum creatinine, BUN, potassium, uric acid, lipids, and bilirubin/liver enzymes, and decrease magnesium. Distinguish drug-induced creatinine rise from graft rejection. Trough results vary with assay method (monoclonal immunoassay vs HPLC) - interpret targets in the context of the assay used.

serious: Structural nephrotoxicity (acute and chronic, dose-related) with significant creatinine/BUN rise
Serious and fatal infections (including opportunistic and viral, e.g., BK virus, CMV, JC virus/PML)
Malignancy - lymphoma/lymphoproliferative disease and skin cancers
Thrombotic microangiopathy / hemolytic-uremic syndrome (glomerular capillary thrombosis)
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), seizures (esp. with hypomagnesemia)
rare: Benign intracranial hypertension / optic disc edema with visual impairment

monitoring: Whole-blood ciclosporin trough concentrations (TDM) - more frequent early after transplant and after any interacting-drug or formulation change
Serum creatinine and renal function repeatedly (RA/psoriasis: creatinine on two occasions before starting, then every 2 weeks for first 3 months then monthly)
Blood pressure at baseline and during therapy
Liver function tests and serum bilirubin
Fasting serum lipids and uric acid
Skin examination and surveillance for infection and malignancy (lymphoma, skin cancer)
counsel: Take twice daily on a consistent schedule with regard to meals; do not change brands or modified/non-modified formulation without your physician's guidance

You are at higher risk of serious infections and of cancers, especially of the skin - report fever, persistent cough, or skin changes; limit sun/UV exposure and use protective clothing and high-SPF sunscreen, and avoid PUVA/UVB if treating psoriasis
Attend all blood pressure checks, blood tests, and drug-level monitoring; report decreased urination, swelling, or unusual bruising/bleeding
Gum overgrowth is common - maintain good oral hygiene and dental care; report excessive hair growth, tremor, or numbness
Tell every provider before starting or stopping any prescription, OTC, herbal (especially St. John's Wort), or supplement product, and avoid live vaccines
The capsules and liquid contain alcohol - avoid additional alcohol; discuss pregnancy and breastfeeding plans with your physician
pk: Immunosuppression develops over days; in RA clinical benefit usually appears at 4-8 weeks
Oral Tmax approximately 1.5-2 hours (modified microemulsion); absorption incomplete and variable
Terminal half-life ~8.4 hours (range 5-18 h); prolonged in severe hepatic impairment
Twice-daily dosing (every 12 hours); extensively CYP3A metabolized, eliminated mainly in bile, only ~6% in urine
Store capsules and oral solution at 20-25 C (68-77 F); keep in original container, protect from extreme temperature; use oral solution within 2 months of opening, do not refrigerate (gel may form)
pearls: Modified (microemulsion, e.g., Neoral/Gengraf) and non-modified (Sandimmune) ciclosporin are NOT bioequivalent - modified has higher, more predictable bioavailability; for the same trough target it gives greater exposure, so never substitute without physician supervision and re-monitor troughs
INN is ciclosporin; US/openFDA generic name is cyclosporine - the molecule is identical

Boxed warning emphasizes specialist-only prescribing, increased serious/fatal infection and malignancy (lymphoma, skin) risk, and structural nephrotoxicity with significant creatinine rises requiring careful TDM and renal monitoring
In RA and psoriasis, abnormal renal function, uncontrolled hypertension, or malignancy are contraindications; do not combine psoriasis therapy with PUVA/UVB, methotrexate, coal tar, or radiation
Statin + ciclosporin markedly raises statin levels - reduce statin dose and watch for myopathy/rhabdomyolysis; St. John's Wort can drop ciclosporin levels and precipitate rejection
Gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism are characteristic ciclosporin effects (contrast with tacrolimus, which more often causes alopecia and diabetes)
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered to keep the 12-hour spacing; if it is close to the next scheduled dose, skip the missed one and resume the regular schedule. Do not double up. Repeated missed doses risk graft rejection or loss of disease control - contact the transplant team or prescriber.
overdose: Experience is limited. Forced emesis and gastric lavage may help within about 2 hours of ingestion. Oral doses up to 10 g (about 150 mg/kg) have caused relatively minor effects (vomiting, drowsiness, headache, tachycardia, and in some patients moderately severe but reversible renal impairment); transient hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity may occur and usually resolve after withdrawal. Serious intoxication has followed accidental parenteral overdose in premature neonates. Ciclosporin is not significantly dialyzable; management is general supportive and symptomatic care.
